steps: Pick a language: C++, Java or Python. Stay with one until you are comfortable.
Create your accounts on LeetCode, Codeforces, CodeChef and GitHub, then add them to your CampusCoders profile.

qa.q: I am a beginner. Where do I start today?
qa.a: Pick a language, finish a basic course such as CS50, and solve one easy problem. Then open Striver's A2Z sheet and begin at step 1.

qa.q: C++, Java or Python?
qa.a: Whichever you will actually practise. C++ is the usual choice for competitive programming, Java for enterprise roles, Python for AI and quick scripting. Interviews accept all three.

qa.q: How many problems are enough?
qa.a: There is no fixed number. When you can spot the pattern in a new medium problem and solve it in 30–40 minutes, you are in good shape.

qa.q: I am in my final year. Is it too late?
qa.a: No. Focus on the SDE sheet, the core subjects and mock interviews, build one strong project, and apply right away.

qa.q: Should I do DSA or development first?
qa.a: Both, in short daily slots. DSA gets you through the screening, and projects get you through the interview and the job.

qa.q: My rank is low. Should I worry?
qa.a: Rank only shows where you are today. Improve your trend week over week and keep going.

sections.heading: Year 1 in detail: build the base
paragraphs: Goal: be comfortable writing code, using Git, and solving easy problems without help.
bullets: Learn: one language (C++, Java or Python), variables, loops, functions, arrays, strings, recursion basics, and Big-O at a simple level.
Learn: Git and GitHub (init, add, commit, branch, push, pull request) and the terminal basics.
Learn: HTML, CSS and a little JavaScript, so you can put a page online.
Practise: 150–200 easy problems across arrays, strings, hashing and maths. Join a few beginner contests.
Build: a calculator, a to-do app, a quiz game and a personal portfolio page. Put each on GitHub with a README.
Milestone by the end of the year: you can solve most easy problems alone, and you have 3–4 small projects online.
Avoid: hopping between languages, watching tutorials without typing the code, and skipping maths and logic.

sections.heading: Year 2 in detail: go deep on the core
paragraphs: Goal: finish the main data structures and algorithms, learn the core subjects, and make your first real projects.
bullets: Learn: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, graphs, hashing, sorting, binary search, recursion, backtracking and starter dynamic programming.
Learn: OOP, DBMS with SQL, operating systems and computer networks as your college teaches them. Revise by solving questions, not by re-reading.
Practise: 250–350 problems, mostly medium. Take part in every weekly contest you can, and upsolve what you missed.
Build: two full projects with a database and login, one of them deployed. Send your first open-source pull request (even a docs fix).
Milestone: you recognise common patterns (two pointers, sliding window, BFS/DFS, DP) and have two deployed projects.
Avoid: starting a hard topic like advanced DP before the basics are solid, and copying solutions without understanding.

sections.heading: Year 3 in detail: prepare for internships and interviews
paragraphs: Goal: be interview-ready for an internship at the end of this year. Most placement and internship cycles start early in the year or even before it.
bullets: Learn: system design basics, low-level design, SQL beyond the basics, OS and networks for interviews, and your chosen role's stack.
Practise: finish a standard SDE sheet, then solve 150+ more medium problems by pattern. Do timed mock rounds every week from the middle of the year.
Build: one larger project that solves a real problem for real users, with tests, a README, a live demo and a short write-up of the trade-offs.
Apply: write the resume in the first month, ask seniors for referrals, apply to internships, and keep a tracking sheet of every application.
Do: at least five mock interviews with friends or seniors, including a behavioural round.
Milestone: a resume with 2–3 strong projects, a profile on LeetCode/Codeforces/GitHub that backs it up, and applications out.
Avoid: waiting until you feel ready to apply, and writing a resume that lists tools instead of what you built.

sections.heading: Year 4 in detail: convert the work into an offer
paragraphs: Goal: get placed or hired, finish your final-year project, and set up your first job well.
bullets: Revise: DSA patterns, core subjects and your projects. Be able to explain every line of every project on your resume.
Do: campus placements, off-campus applications, referrals and cold emails in parallel. One channel is rarely enough.
Practise: weekly mock interviews, company-specific question lists, and a timed online-assessment routine.
Build: a strong final-year project, preferably linked to your target role, with a demo you can show in two minutes.
Learn: how offers work: CTC versus in-hand pay, notice periods, joining dates, and what to ask before you accept.
Prepare: for the first job. Read the stack of the company you joined, and learn its tools and Git workflow before day one.
Milestone: one or more offers, a repo and demo for the final-year project, and a plan for your first 90 days.
Avoid: stopping practice after one rejection, accepting the first offer without reading it, and burning out in the last semester.

paragraphs: Most people I have worked with did not follow a perfect plan. What they shared was a habit of shipping small things and learning from the result.

sections.heading: How to practise properly
steps: Learn the topic first. Watch or read one lesson, then solve the easy problems of that topic the same day.
Think before you look. Give each problem 20–30 minutes: restate it, try small examples, write the brute force, then improve it.
Read the editorial only after a real attempt. Then close it and code the solution from memory. Copying code teaches nothing.
Write down what you learned: the pattern, the trick, and why your first idea failed.
Revise on a schedule. Re-solve a problem after 3 days, 2 weeks and 2 months. Mark the ones you got wrong.
Always state the time and space complexity out loud.
Do not jump ahead. Finish a topic before starting the next.

sections.heading: The A2Z order
paragraphs: Basics and pattern printing, sorting, arrays, binary search, strings, linked lists, recursion and backtracking, bit manipulation, stacks and queues, sliding window and two pointers, heaps, greedy, binary trees, binary search trees, graphs, dynamic programming, tries.

sections.heading: Targets
paragraphs: These are rough guides, not rules. About 150 LeetCode problems and a rating of 1400+ in LeetCode contests makes a good campus placement profile. Top product companies tend to expect 300+ problems and some Codeforces or CodeChef contest history.

sections.heading: Competitive programming

Join every LeetCode weekly and biweekly contest, and one Codeforces Div. 3 or Div. 4 round a week.
After each contest, upsolve: solve the problems you missed, even though the contest is over. This is where most of the improvement comes from.
Aim to solve problems A and B quickly and accurately before chasing C.
Read how top-rated people solved the problems you could not.

sections.heading: From an SDE's desk
paragraphs: On the job you will rarely write a red-black tree. You will pick the right structure, spot a hidden O(n²), and explain why a query is slow. That is what DSA practice buys you.
bullets: The most common real use: choose between a list, a set and a map. Knowing the cost of each avoids slow code before it is written.
A nested loop over two lists that grew is the classic production slowdown. Big-O thinking catches it in review.
Interviews test DSA because it is a fair, comparable signal. Treat it as a skill to build, not as the job itself.
Read other people's solutions after you have tried. The goal is to see a cleaner idea, not to copy a trick.

Look at the input shape: a sorted array, a string, a tree, a graph, intervals or a stream.
Look at the ask: longest, shortest, count of ways, minimum or maximum, all possibilities, or does it exist.
Write the brute force and find where it repeats work. That repeated work is what the pattern removes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes in DSA problems
bullets: Coding before you understand the examples and the edge cases.
Forgetting empty input, a single element, duplicates, negative numbers and overflow.
Off-by-one errors in binary search and sliding windows. Decide whether your range is inclusive or exclusive and stay consistent.
Modifying a collection while looping over it.
Passing a shared list into recursion without copying it when you save a result.
Using recursion on a deep input without thinking about the stack limit.
Stating the wrong complexity, such as ignoring the cost of string slicing or sorting.

sections.heading: From an SDE's desk
paragraphs: Patterns are how experienced engineers recognise a problem fast. The same shapes show up in real code: windows over a stream, graphs of dependencies, intervals in a calendar.
bullets: Dependency order in a build tool is a topological sort. Scheduling meetings is interval merging. Rate limiting is a sliding window.
When two approaches both work, pick the one a teammate can read in a minute. Clever code costs more to maintain than it saves.
Write the brute force first, state its cost, then improve. It is also how you should approach a real performance problem.

code.title: Two pointers on a sorted array (pair with a given sum): O(n) time, O(1) space
Sliding window (longest substring without repeating characters): O(n)
Prefix sums with a hash map (number of subarrays with sum k): O(n)
code.text:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = {0: 1}          # prefix sum -> times seen
    s = result = 0
    for x in nums:
        s += x
        result += count.get(s - k, 0)   # earlier prefix = s - k
        count[s] = count.get(s, 0) + 1
    return result

Binary search on the answer (minimum eating speed so all piles finish in h hours)

bullets: Off-by-one errors live in binary search. Decide once whether your range is [lo, hi) or [lo, hi], and keep every line consistent with it.
For sliding window, ask: what makes the window invalid, and how do I shrink it? If you cannot answer, it is not a sliding-window problem.
Prefix sums turn 'sum of a range' into a subtraction. Whenever you see 'subarray sum', think prefix sums plus a map.

code.title: Monotonic stack (days until a warmer temperature): O(n), each index pushed and popped once
BFS (shortest distance in an unweighted graph): O(V + E)
DFS on a grid (number of islands): O(rows x cols)
Topological sort with Kahn's algorithm (course order): O(V + E)
code.text:
from collections import deque

def topo_order(n, edges):               # edge (a, b): a must come before b
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indegree = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:
        graph[a].append(b)
        indegree[b] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []   # empty list means a cycle

code.title: Dijkstra with a heap (shortest paths, non-negative weights): O((V + E) log V)
Union-find with path compression and union by size: near O(1) per operation

bullets: Use BFS for fewest steps in an unweighted graph. Use Dijkstra when edges have weights, and never with negative weights.
Recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a deep input. Use an explicit stack when depth could reach thousands.
A cycle in a dependency graph means no valid order. Topological sort tells you that for free.

sections.heading: Code templates: backtracking and dynamic programming

code.title: Backtracking (all subsets): choose, explore, un-choose. O(2^n)
code.text:
def subsets(nums):
    result, path = [], []

    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])      # copy, the list keeps changing
            return
        go(i + 1)                       # skip nums[i]
        path.append(nums[i])            # take nums[i]
        go(i + 1)
        path.pop()                      # undo

    go(0)
    return result

Why

Customer details repeat on every row, so changing a city means updating many rows. That is an update anomaly. Deleting the only order for a product deletes the product, a delete anomaly. Normalisation splits the table so each fact is stored once.

NULL is not equal to anything, even NULL. Use IS NULL, and remember that COUNT(col) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) does not.

sections.heading: DBMS in depth: indexes, query plans and transactions
paragraphs: An index is usually a B+ tree: sorted, shallow and good at equality and range lookups. A composite index on (customer_id, created_at) helps queries that filter on customer_id, or on customer_id and then created_at. It does not help a query that filters only on created_at. This is the left-most prefix rule.

code.title: Create an index and read the plan
A transaction: both updates happen or neither does

bullets: ACID: atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (rules hold), isolation (transactions do not see each other's half-done work) and durability (committed data survives a crash).
Indexes speed up reads but slow writes and use space. Index the columns you filter, join and sort on, not every column.
Functions on an indexed column, such as WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x', can stop the index being used. Index the expression, or store it normalised.
A deadlock happens when two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds. Databases detect it and abort one. Reduce the risk by locking rows in a consistent order and keeping transactions short.
SQL versus NoSQL is about access patterns. Relational databases suit related data and strong consistency. Key-value, document and wide-column stores suit specific scale or shape needs.

Process

bullets: A process moves between states: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked) and terminated. A context switch saves one task's registers and loads another's, which costs time.
FCFS is simple but a long job can block short ones (the convoy effect). SJF minimises average waiting time but can starve long jobs and needs a guess of run time.
Round robin gives each task a time slice. A tiny slice wastes time switching, and a huge one behaves like FCFS.
Priority scheduling can starve low-priority tasks. Aging raises the priority of a task the longer it waits.
Real operating systems use a mix, such as multilevel feedback queues, to favour interactive tasks and still be fair.

How to break it

Use shareable resources where you can

bullets: A mutex lets one task into a critical section. A semaphore is a counter that lets up to N tasks in. A condition variable lets tasks wait until something becomes true.
Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages. A page table maps virtual pages to physical frames, and the TLB caches recent translations.
A page fault happens when a page is not in memory. The OS loads it from disk, which is thousands of times slower than memory.
Thrashing is when a system spends more time swapping pages than doing work, because too many tasks compete for too little memory.
Common page replacement choices are FIFO, LRU and clock. LRU performs well but costs bookkeeping to track recency.
Virtual memory lets each process think it has its own large, continuous address space and keeps processes isolated from each other.

sections.heading: Computer networks in depth: from a URL to a response
steps: The browser checks its caches, then asks a DNS resolver to turn the domain into an IP address. The resolver walks root, top-level domain and authoritative servers if it has no cached answer.
The browser opens a TCP connection with a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
For HTTPS, a TLS handshake follows: the server proves its identity with a certificate, and both sides agree on session keys for encrypted traffic.
The browser sends an HTTP request: a method, a path, headers (host, cookies, accept) and sometimes a body.
A load balancer or reverse proxy forwards the request to an application server, which may call caches and databases.
The server returns a response with a status code, headers and a body. The browser parses HTML, then fetches CSS, JavaScript and images, often in parallel and over a reused connection.
The browser builds the DOM and renders the page. Cached files and CDNs make later visits faster.

bullets: TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery with retransmission, flow control and congestion control. UDP skips all that for speed, which suits video calls, games and DNS.
Common HTTP status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301 and 302 redirects, 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests, 500 server error, 503 unavailable.
GET reads and should not change data. POST creates. PUT replaces. PATCH changes part of a resource. DELETE removes. GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (on UDP) to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.
A cookie stores small data in the browser and sends it back with each request. Use HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags for session cookies.
CORS is a browser rule: a page can read a cross-origin response only if the server allows it with the right headers.

qa.q: What is normalisation, and why do we do it?
qa.a: It is organising tables so each fact is stored once, to avoid update, insert and delete anomalies. 1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF removes partial dependencies on a key, 3NF removes dependencies between non-key columns, and BCNF tightens 3NF.

qa.q: What are the ACID properties?
qa.a: Atomicity: a transaction happens fully or not at all. Consistency: it moves the database from one valid state to another. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work. Durability: once committed, it survives a crash.

qa.q: Primary key, candidate key, foreign key: what is the difference?
qa.a: A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that identifies a row. The primary key is the candidate you choose, and it cannot be null. A foreign key is a column that refers to a primary key in another table, to enforce a relationship.

qa.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
qa.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can use functions such as COUNT and SUM.

qa.q: Explain INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins.
qa.a: INNER keeps only rows that match on both sides. LEFT keeps all rows from the left table and fills nulls where nothing matches. RIGHT is the mirror. FULL keeps all rows from both sides.

qa.q: What is an index, and what does it cost?
qa.a: An index is a separate structure, usually a B+ tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the table. It speeds up reads, but it uses space and slows down inserts, updates and deletes, because it must be maintained.

qa.q: What are the transaction isolation levels?
qa.a: Read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serialisable. Higher levels prevent more anomalies (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allow less concurrency.

qa.q: How is DELETE different from TRUNCATE and DROP?
qa.a: DELETE removes chosen rows and can be rolled back and filtered. TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly and resets the table. DROP removes the table itself, with its structure.

qa.q: SQL or NoSQL?
qa.a: Choose SQL when you need relations, transactions and a fixed schema. Choose NoSQL when you need flexible documents, simple key-based access or horizontal scale, and can accept weaker consistency. Many systems use both.

qa.q: How would you find the second highest salary?
qa.a: Use a subquery on the maximum below the maximum, or DENSE_RANK() over salary descending and select rank 2. The window-function version also handles ties and the top N.

qa.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
qa.a: A process is a running program with its own memory space. Threads are lightweight units of execution inside a process that share its memory, so they communicate easily but can interfere with each other.

qa.q: What is a deadlock, and how can it be prevented?
qa.a: Processes wait for each other's resources forever. It needs four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and circular wait. Break any one, for example by acquiring locks in a fixed order, to prevent it.

qa.q: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
qa.a: A mutex lets one thread at a time into a critical section and is owned by the thread that locks it. A semaphore holds a count, so it lets up to N threads in and can signal between threads.

qa.q: Explain paging and virtual memory.
qa.a: Memory is divided into fixed-size pages, and a page table maps virtual addresses to physical frames. Virtual memory lets a process use more memory than is physically present by keeping rarely used pages on disk.

qa.q: What is a page fault, and what is thrashing?
qa.a: A page fault happens when a program touches a page that is not in memory, so the OS loads it from disk. Thrashing is when the system spends most of its time swapping pages instead of doing work.

qa.q: Name some CPU scheduling algorithms.
qa.a: First come first served, shortest job first, round robin, priority scheduling and multilevel queues. Round robin gives fair time slices, and shortest job first minimises average waiting time but can starve long jobs.

qa.q: What is a context switch?
qa.a: The CPU saves the state of the running process or thread and loads the state of another. It enables multitasking, but it has a cost, so too many switches waste time.

qa.q: What is a system call?
qa.a: The way a user program asks the kernel to do something privileged, such as reading a file or creating a process. It switches from user mode to kernel mode and back.

qa.q: What happens when you type a URL into a browser?
qa.a: The browser looks up the IP address through DNS, opens a TCP connection (and a TLS handshake for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, the server returns a response, and the browser parses the HTML and loads the other resources to render the page.

qa.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
qa.a: TCP is connection-based and reliable: it orders data, retransmits lost packets and controls congestion. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantee, so it is faster and used for video calls, games and DNS.

qa.q: Explain the TCP three-way handshake.
qa.a: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. Both sides now agree on starting sequence numbers and the connection is open.

qa.q: What are the layers of the OSI and TCP/IP models?
qa.a: OSI has seven: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. TCP/IP groups these into four: link, internet, transport and application.

qa.q: How does HTTPS work?
qa.a: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. The server shows a certificate, the client verifies it, and both agree on keys for encrypted communication. It protects against eavesdropping and tampering.

qa.q: What is DNS?
qa.a: The system that turns names like example.com into IP addresses. A resolver asks the root, the top-level domain and the authoritative servers, and caches the answers.

qa.q: What is the difference between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?
qa.a: HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection. HTTP/3 does the same over QUIC (on UDP) to avoid head-of-line blocking at the transport level.

qa.q: What is the difference between GET and POST, and what do the status codes mean?
qa.a: GET reads data and should have no side effects, while POST sends data to create or change something. 2xx means success, 3xx redirect, 4xx a client error (such as 404 or 401) and 5xx a server error.

qa.q: What are the four pillars of OOP?
qa.a: Encapsulation: hide data behind methods. Abstraction: expose only what matters. Inheritance: reuse and extend behaviour. Polymorphism: one interface, many behaviours.

qa.q: Abstract class or interface?
qa.a: An interface defines a contract with no state and can be implemented by any class. An abstract class can share state and partial code among related classes. Use an interface for 'can do', and an abstract class for 'is a'.

qa.q: What does SOLID stand for?
qa.a: Single responsibility, open for extension and closed for modification, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, and dependency inversion. Together they keep code easy to change.

qa.q: Overloading or overriding?
qa.a: Overloading is several methods with the same name and different parameters, decided at compile time. Overriding is a subclass changing an inherited method, decided at run time.

qa.q: Composition or inheritance?
qa.a: Prefer composition: build objects from smaller parts. Inheritance creates tight coupling and fragile hierarchies, so use it only for a true 'is a' relationship.

qa.q: Name a few design patterns and when you would use them.
qa.a: Singleton for one shared instance, Factory to create objects without naming the class, Observer to notify many listeners, Strategy to swap algorithms, and Decorator to add behaviour without subclassing.

qa.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
qa.a: Authentication proves who you are. Authorisation decides what you may do once known.

qa.q: Sessions or JWTs?
qa.a: A session keeps state on the server and gives the client an identifier in a cookie, so it is easy to revoke. A JWT is a signed token holding claims, so the server stays stateless, but revoking it before it expires is harder.

qa.q: What is REST?
qa.a: An API style where URLs name resources and HTTP verbs act on them: GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update and DELETE to remove, with stateless requests.

qa.q: What is CORS?
qa.a: A browser rule that stops a page from one origin reading responses from another unless the server says so with headers. It protects users, and does not protect the server itself.

qa.q: How do you prevent SQL injection?
qa.a: Never build queries by joining user input into a string. Use parameterised queries or an ORM, validate input and give the database user only the permissions it needs.

qa.q: What is caching, and what is the risk?
qa.a: Keeping a copy of data that is expensive to compute or fetch. The risk is stale data, so you need a plan for expiry and invalidation.

sections.heading: Behavioural questions
paragraphs: Use the STAR shape: Situation, Task, Action and Result. Keep each answer to about two minutes, say 'I' for what you did, and end with a result and what you learned.

qa.q: Tell me about yourself.
qa.a: Give a 60-second summary: who you are, what you study, one or two projects or results that matter, and why you want this role. Do not recite your resume.

qa.q: Tell me about a project you are proud of.
qa.a: Describe the problem, your part, one technical decision and why you made it, a bug that taught you something, and the result, ideally with a number.

qa.q: Describe a time you failed.
qa.a: Choose a real, small failure. Say what you did wrong, how you fixed it and what you do differently now. Do not blame others.

qa.q: How do you handle disagreement in a team?
qa.a: Listen first, explain your reasoning with evidence, find the goal you share, and accept the team's decision once it is made.

qa.q: Why do you want to work here?
qa.a: Name something specific: the product, the technology, the team or the problem. Link it to what you want to learn. Research before the interview.

qa.q: Do you have any questions for us?
qa.a: Always ask. For example: what does the first three months look like, how do you review code, what is the hardest problem the team has now, and how do new people get mentored?

qa.q: Array versus linked list: when would you choose each?
qa.a: Arrays give O(1) access by index and good cache use, but inserting in the middle costs O(n) and resizing copies data. Linked lists insert or delete in O(1) once you hold the node, but access is O(n) and each node has pointer overhead. Choose an array by default and a linked list when you do many insertions and deletions in the middle and rarely index.

qa.q: How does a hash map work, and what happens on a collision?
qa.a: A hash function maps a key to a bucket index. Two keys can land in the same bucket, which is a collision. Common fixes are chaining (each bucket holds a list) and open addressing (probe for the next free slot). Lookup is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case. A resize keeps the load factor low.

qa.q: Compare BFS and DFS. When is each the right choice?
qa.a: BFS explores level by level with a queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. DFS goes deep with a stack or recursion and suits cycle detection, topological sort, connected components and backtracking. Both are O(V+E).

qa.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
qa.a: A stack is last in, first out (push and pop at one end). A queue is first in, first out (add at the back, remove from the front). Stacks suit undo, recursion and parsing. Queues suit scheduling and BFS.

qa.q: What is dynamic programming, and how do you start a DP problem?
qa.a: DP solves a problem by combining answers to overlapping subproblems and storing them to avoid repeat work. Start by defining the state in words, write the recurrence between states, set the base cases, choose the order (top-down with memoisation or bottom-up with a table), then see if you can shrink the space.

qa.q: Why is quicksort usually faster than merge sort in practice, even though its worst case is worse?
qa.a: Quicksort sorts in place with good cache behaviour and small constants, and a random or median pivot makes the O(n²) case very unlikely. Merge sort always runs in O(n log n) and is stable but needs O(n) extra space.

qa.q: What is a balanced binary search tree, and why does balance matter?
qa.a: A balanced BST keeps its height near log n, so search, insert and delete stay O(log n). Without balance, sorted inserts turn the tree into a list with O(n) operations. AVL and red-black trees keep balance with rotations.

qa.q: What does amortised O(1) mean?
qa.a: It means the average cost per operation over a long sequence is constant, even if a few operations are expensive. Appending to a dynamic array is the usual example: most appends are O(1), and an occasional resize costs O(n), but spread over all appends the average is O(1).

qa.q: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
qa.a: Merge joins two branches with a merge commit and keeps the true history. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history but rewriting those commits. Do not rebase commits that others already use.

qa.q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
qa.a: Fetch downloads new commits and updates remote-tracking branches without changing your working branch. Pull is a fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch.

qa.q: What are unit, integration and end-to-end tests?
qa.a: Unit tests check one function or class in isolation. Integration tests check that parts work together, such as an API with its database. End-to-end tests drive the whole system the way a user would. Keep many unit tests, fewer integration tests and a few end-to-end tests.

qa.q: What is CI/CD?
qa.a: Continuous integration builds and tests every change automatically so problems show up early. Continuous delivery or deployment then releases the passing build, either with one click or fully automatically.

qa.q: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
qa.a: A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system on virtual hardware. A container shares the host kernel and isolates only the process and its files, so it starts faster and uses less memory.

sections.heading: How ready are you in each year?

head: Year
A fair interview-readiness target
rows: Explain your language's basics and solve easy problems. No interviews yet, just build confidence.
Answer basic OOP, DBMS and OS questions, and solve medium problems with hints.
Answer core-subject questions clearly, solve mediums alone, and explain every project you list.
Handle a full loop: coding, core subjects, a design discussion, projects and a behavioural round.

sections.heading: From an SDE's desk
paragraphs: As someone who sits on the interviewer side: we are not checking if you memorised an answer. We want to see how you think and whether we would enjoy solving problems with you.
bullets: Say your thinking aloud. A reasoned wrong answer scores better than a silent right one.
Ask a clarifying question before you start. It signals that you would ask in a real ticket as well.
If you do not know, say so, then reason from what you do know. Bluffing is easy to spot and costs trust.
Honest answers about projects win. Be ready to go two levels deeper on anything on your resume.

qa.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
qa.a: A process has its own memory space and resources. Threads inside a process share its memory, so they are cheaper to create and to switch between, but they need synchronisation and a crash in one can bring down the process.

qa.q: What is a context switch, and why is it expensive?
qa.a: It is when the CPU stops one task and starts another, saving and restoring registers and other state. It costs time directly and also hurts caches, because the new task's data is not warm.

qa.q: What are the four conditions for deadlock?
qa.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. All four must hold. Breaking any one prevents deadlock, for example by locking in a fixed order to avoid circular wait.

qa.q: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
qa.a: A mutex is a lock owned by one thread at a time, used to protect a critical section. A semaphore is a counter that allows up to N holders and can be signalled by a different thread, used to limit access or to coordinate.

qa.q: What is virtual memory?
qa.a: A technique that gives every process its own large address space, mapped to physical memory and disk by the OS and hardware. It gives isolation, lets programs use more than physical RAM, and simplifies loading.

qa.q: What is a page fault?
qa.a: An access to a page that is not currently in physical memory. The OS finds the page on disk, loads it into a frame, updates the page table and restarts the instruction.

qa.q: What is thrashing?
qa.a: When the system spends most of its time moving pages between memory and disk because processes need more memory than is available, so little real work is done. Fix by reducing the number of active processes or adding memory.

qa.q: What is starvation, and how does aging help?
qa.a: Starvation is when a task never gets a resource because others keep getting it first. Aging gradually raises a waiting task's priority so it eventually runs.

qa.q: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
qa.a: Kernel mode can run privileged instructions and access all hardware and memory. User mode is restricted. Programs enter kernel mode only through system calls, which protects the system from faulty or hostile programs.

qa.q: What is a zombie process?
qa.a: A process that has finished but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not yet read its exit status. The parent should call wait to clean it up.

qa.q: Explain the TCP three-way handshake.
qa.a: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. Both sides now agree on starting sequence numbers and the connection is open. Closing uses FIN and ACK messages from each side.

qa.q: TCP versus UDP: when would you choose each?
qa.a: TCP when you need reliable, ordered delivery, such as web pages, files and APIs. UDP when speed matters more than perfect delivery or you handle loss yourself, such as live video, games and DNS.

qa.q: How does DNS work?
qa.a: A resolver checks its cache, then asks root servers, then the top-level domain servers, then the authoritative server for the domain, which returns the IP address. Answers are cached for a time to live.

qa.q: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
qa.a: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. TLS encrypts traffic, verifies the server's identity with a certificate and protects against tampering.

qa.q: What is the difference between GET and POST?
qa.a: GET requests data and should not change anything, so it can be cached and bookmarked. POST sends data to create or change something, and its body is not part of the URL. Neither is secure by itself, because security comes from HTTPS and the server.

qa.q: What is a load balancer?
qa.a: A component that spreads requests across servers, checks their health and removes failed ones, and may end TLS. It can work at layer 4 (connections) or layer 7 (HTTP content).

qa.q: What is NAT?
qa.a: Network address translation lets many devices in a private network share one public IP address. The router rewrites addresses and ports and remembers the mapping for replies.

qa.q: What is the difference between a hub, a switch and a router?
qa.a: A hub repeats traffic to all ports. A switch forwards frames only to the right port using MAC addresses. A router connects different networks and forwards packets using IP addresses.

qa.q: What is a CDN?
qa.a: A content delivery network is a set of servers around the world that cache static content close to users, giving lower latency and taking load off your origin server.

qa.q: What is the difference between a cookie, a session and a token?
qa.a: A cookie is data the browser stores and sends back. A session is server-side state, usually found by an ID kept in a cookie. A token, such as a JWT, carries signed claims that the server can check without looking up state.

qa.q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
qa.a: DELETE removes selected rows, can use WHERE and can be rolled back in a transaction. TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly and keeps the table. DROP removes the table itself, including structure and data.

qa.q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
qa.a: A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows, so a table has only one. A non-clustered index is a separate structure with pointers to the rows, and a table can have many.

qa.q: What is a view, and what is a materialised view?
qa.a: A view is a stored query that behaves like a table. A materialised view stores its result and must be refreshed, which makes reads fast but adds staleness.

qa.q: What is a stored procedure, and when would you avoid one?
qa.a: A stored procedure is code saved inside the database. It can reduce round trips and centralise logic, but it is harder to version, test and move between databases, so many teams keep business logic in application code.

qa.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
qa.a: UNION combines results and removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash. UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you need deduplication.

qa.q: What is a correlated subquery?
qa.a: A subquery that refers to a column of the outer query, so it runs once per outer row. It can be slow, and is often rewritten as a join or a window function.

qa.q: How would you find the Nth highest salary?
qa.a: Use DENSE_RANK() over salary descending in a subquery and filter for rank N. An older approach is ORDER BY salary DESC with LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1, which does not handle ties the same way.

qa.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
qa.a: Running one query for a list and then one more per item. Fix it with a join, or by fetching all related rows in one batched query.

qa.q: What is database replication, and what is replication lag?
qa.a: Replication copies data from a primary to replicas for read scaling and failover. Lag is the delay before a change reaches a replica, so a read from a replica can briefly return old data.

qa.q: When would you pick NoSQL over SQL?
qa.a: When the data shape is flexible, when you need very high write volume or horizontal scale, or when access is simple key-based. Pick SQL when you need joins, transactions and a stable schema.

qa.q: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
qa.a: An interface describes what a type can do and has no state, so a class can implement many. An abstract class can hold shared state and partial code but a class can usually extend only one. Prefer interfaces for contracts and abstract classes for shared base behaviour.

qa.q: What is polymorphism? Give an example.
qa.a: One interface with different behaviour depending on the object. A Shape list where each item has an area() method gives the right area for circles and rectangles without checking types.

qa.q: Composition versus inheritance: which do you prefer?
qa.a: Composition. It keeps parts independent and swappable, while deep inheritance couples a subclass tightly to its parent. Use inheritance for a true 'is a' relationship with stable behaviour.

qa.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
qa.a: Overloading is several methods with the same name but different parameters, resolved at compile time. Overriding is a subclass replacing a parent's method with the same signature, resolved at run time.

qa.q: What is the singleton pattern, and what are its problems?
qa.a: A class that allows one instance with global access. It hides dependencies, makes tests harder and can cause trouble with threads. Prefer passing a single instance in through the constructor.

qa.q: What is dependency injection?
qa.a: Giving an object the things it needs from outside instead of letting it create them. It makes code easier to test and to change, for example by passing a fake database in a test.

qa.q: What is the difference between shallow and deep copy?
qa.a: A shallow copy duplicates the outer object but shares inner objects. A deep copy duplicates everything, so changes to the copy never affect the original.

qa.q: What does 'program to an interface, not an implementation' mean?
qa.a: Depend on a contract, not a concrete class, so you can swap the implementation without changing the callers.

qa.q: Design a parking lot. How would you start?
qa.a: Ask about vehicle types, floors, pricing and payment. Identify nouns as classes (ParkingLot, Level, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket) and behaviours as methods (park, unpark, calculateFee). Keep spot assignment and pricing as separate strategies so each can change.

qa.q: What is a race condition, and how do you avoid it?
qa.a: A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads touching shared data. Avoid it by not sharing mutable state, or by protecting it with locks, atomic operations or immutable data.

qa.q: How do you design a rate limiter?
qa.a: Choose an algorithm (token bucket is a good default), key it by user or IP, store counters in a shared fast store such as Redis, return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and decide what to do if the store fails, usually allowing the request.

qa.q: How would you design a URL shortener?
qa.a: Generate a unique short code from a counter encoded in base62, store code to URL, redirect on read, cache hot links and rate-limit creation. Reads far outnumber writes, so scale reads with caches and replicas.

qa.q: How do you scale a read-heavy service?
qa.a: Cache, add read replicas, use a CDN for static data, add indexes, and precompute results that are expensive to build.

qa.q: How do you scale a write-heavy service?
qa.a: Batch and queue writes, partition or shard the data, choose a store built for high write throughput, and reduce write amplification such as extra indexes.

qa.q: What is eventual consistency, and when is it fine?
qa.a: Replicas converge after a delay without a guarantee that every read is the latest. It suits feeds, likes and counters, and does not suit payments or inventory that must not oversell.

qa.q: How would you make a payment API safe to retry?
qa.a: Require an idempotency key. Store the result of the first request under that key, and return the same result for repeats, so a retry never charges twice.

qa.q: Monolith or microservices?
qa.a: Start with a well-structured monolith. Split out a service when a part needs to scale, deploy or be owned separately. Microservices add network failures, distributed data and operational cost.

qa.q: How do you find the bottleneck in a slow system?
qa.a: Measure. Look at latency percentiles, then trace a slow request through each hop, and check CPU, memory, database queries and queues. Fix the biggest cost first, and measure again.

pages.label: System design
pages.title: System design basics
pages.intro: System design asks how you would build something that many people use: what the parts are, how they talk, and what breaks first. Start after you are comfortable with DSA and databases. For freshers the bar is lower: show clear thinking, not a perfect architecture.

sections.heading: When it matters
bullets: Freshers: some product companies ask a light design question, such as a URL shortener or a parking lot. Many ask only low-level design (classes and objects).
1–3 years of experience: expect one full design round.
Senior roles: design is the main round.
Even when it is not asked, it makes you a better developer, because you stop writing code that cannot scale.

sections.heading: A framework for any design question
steps: Clarify the requirements. What must it do (functional), and how well (speed, availability, scale)? Ask who the users are and how many.
Estimate the scale: requests per second, data stored per day, read-to-write ratio. Rough numbers are enough.
Define the API: the main endpoints and what they take and return.
Sketch the data model: the main entities and which database fits.
Draw the high-level design: clients, load balancer, services, database, cache, queue.
Go deeper on one or two parts the interviewer cares about, such as how to generate unique IDs or how to fan out a feed.
Discuss bottlenecks and trade-offs: single points of failure, hot keys, consistency versus availability.
Summarise, and say what you would improve with more time.

head: Block
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Spreads requests over several servers and drops unhealthy ones
One server cannot handle the traffic, or you want no single point of failure
Keeps hot data in memory for quick reads
Reads are far more frequent than writes, or a query is slow
Serves static files from servers near the user
Images, videos and scripts are slow for faraway users
Stores structured data with transactions and joins
You need consistency, relations and flexible queries
Scales out for simple access patterns
Huge volume, a flexible schema, or lookups by key
You want more read capacity or failover
Splits data over servers by a key
One database cannot hold or serve all the data
Holds work to be done later, decoupling producers and consumers
Spikes, slow tasks such as emails, or several consumers of an event
A single entry point for authentication, routing and rate limits
Many services sit behind one public API
Cheap storage for files and large blobs
SQL LIKE queries become slow or too limited

sections.heading: Numbers worth remembering

head: Quantity
Rough value
rows: About 12 requests per second on average
Network round trip in one data centre
A typical row or small JSON object
Plan for 2 to 10 times the average

paragraphs: You are not expected to be exact. Show that you can reason: 10 million users, 10% active a day, 5 actions each, is 5 million writes a day, or about 60 per second on average.

sections.heading: Key trade-offs

head: Choice
What you gain
What you pay
rows: Stale data, and invalidation is hard
Replicas may lag, so reads can be stale
Cross-shard queries and rebalancing are hard
Eventual results, retries and duplicates to handle
Network failures, deployment and debugging cost
Slower, and less available during failures
Users may briefly see old data

paragraphs: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a system must choose between consistency and availability. Banks choose consistency. Social feeds usually choose availability.

head: Design
Key ideas to cover
rows: Unique ID or hash generation, base62 encoding, a read-heavy cache, a redirect with 301 or 302, expiry, and click analytics
Token bucket or sliding window, counters in Redis, per-user and per-IP limits, and what happens across several servers
WebSockets, message ordering, delivery receipts, offline storage, group chats and fan-out
Fan-out on write versus on read, ranking, a cache for hot users, and pagination
A queue, templates, retries, deduplication, user preferences and several channels
Chunked uploads, metadata separate from blobs, sync, versioning and deduplication
Location updates, geospatial indexing, matching, surge pricing and payments
Encoding to several resolutions, a CDN, adaptive bitrate and a recommendation service

sections.heading: Low-level design (object-oriented design)
paragraphs: Many fresher interviews ask for classes and relationships instead of servers. The aim is clean, extensible code.
bullets: Practise: parking lot, library management, elevator, tic-tac-toe, chess, a vending machine, a food ordering app and an ATM.
Steps: list the requirements, identify the objects (nouns), write their behaviour (verbs), draw the relationships, then code the core classes.
Use SOLID principles and a design pattern only where it fits, for example Strategy for pricing rules or State for a vending machine.
Handle concurrency and edge cases at the end, and say which assumptions you made.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Jumping to the architecture without asking questions.
Adding Kafka, Kubernetes and microservices to a problem that needs one database.
Ignoring data: no schema, no estimate of size.
Not discussing failure: what happens when a server, a database or a network link goes down.
Saying 'use a cache' without saying what is cached, for how long and how it is invalidated.
Going quiet. Explain your thinking all the time.

sections.heading: Worked example: a URL shortener
steps: Clarify: users create a short link for a long URL and are redirected when they open it. Ask about custom aliases, expiry, analytics and expected traffic.
Estimate: suppose 100 million new links a month and a read-to-write ratio of 100:1. That is roughly 40 writes a second and 4,000 reads a second on average, and more at peak.
API: POST /links with the long URL returns a short code. GET /{code} returns a redirect (HTTP 301 or 302).
Data: one table with code (primary key), long URL, created time, expiry and owner. A key-value store or a SQL table with an index on code both work.
Generate the code: use a counter encoded in base62, or hash the URL and check for collisions. A counter is simple and has no collisions, but needs care when many servers run.
Scale reads: put a cache such as Redis in front of the database, because the same popular links are read again and again. Add a CDN or edge cache if the traffic is global.
Scale writes: split the data by code range or hash. Give each application server a block of counter values so servers do not wait on each other.
Extras: rate-limit creation, check links for abuse, and log clicks through a queue so analytics never slow down a redirect.
Trade-offs to mention: 301 is cached by browsers and cuts load but hides later clicks. 302 lets you count every click. Random codes are harder to guess than counters.

sections.heading: Which year to learn system design
bullets: Years 1–2: learn how the web, databases and caches work. You do not need to design systems yet.
Year 3: learn the framework, building blocks and a few classic designs. Practise saying your thinking aloud.
Year 4: practise full designs against a timer, and rehearse low-level design for the companies that ask for it.

sections.heading: From an SDE's desk
paragraphs: In real teams, system design is mostly deciding what not to build. The best design is the simplest one that meets today's load with a clear path to the next stage.
bullets: Start with one server and one database. Add a cache, a queue or a new service only when a measured problem asks for it.
Every box you add is something that can fail at 3 am and something a teammate must learn. Count that cost.
Write the design down before building it, even a one-page note. Many bad ideas die on paper cheaply.
Numbers beat opinions. Estimate load and storage, then check against real metrics after launch.

sections.heading: Deep dive: caching

head: Strategy
How it works
Good for
Watch out for
rows: App checks the cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache.
Read-heavy data, the most common choice.
Stale data after writes. Delete or update the key on write.
The cache itself loads from the database on a miss.
Needs a cache that supports it.
Writes go to the cache and the database together.
Data that is read right after it is written.
Writes go to the cache and are saved to the database later.
Data loss if the cache fails before saving.

code.title: Cache-aside with expiry (a plain dict stands in for Redis)
code.text:
import time

cache = {}                              # key -> (value, expires_at)
TTL = 60                                # seconds

def get_user(user_id, db):
    hit = cache.get(user_id)
    if hit and hit[1] > time.time():
        return hit[0]                   # cache hit
    user = db.fetch_user(user_id)       # cache miss: go to the source
    cache[user_id] = (user, time.time() + TTL)
    return user

def update_user(user_id, data, db):
    db.save_user(user_id, data)
    cache.pop(user_id, None)            # invalidate so the next read is fresh

code.title: An LRU cache: evict the least recently used item

bullets: Cache what is read often and changes rarely. Do not cache what is cheap to compute or must always be exact, such as an account balance.
Pick a time to live (TTL) on purpose. Short TTLs mean fresher data and more database load.
Cache stampede: a popular key expires and many requests hit the database at once. Add random jitter to TTLs, or let one request rebuild while the others wait.
Eviction policies: LRU (least recently used), LFU (least frequently used) and FIFO. LRU is the usual default.
Layers: the browser cache, a CDN for static files, an application cache such as Redis, and the database's own buffers.

sections.heading: Deep dive: scaling the database
steps: Add indexes and fix slow queries first. This is the cheapest and biggest win.
Add a cache for repeated reads.
Add read replicas: one primary takes writes, copies take reads. Replication lag means a replica can briefly serve old data.
Scale vertically (a bigger machine) while that is simpler than anything else.
Partition large tables, for example by date, so queries touch less data.
Shard: split data across several databases by a key such as user_id. It works, but cross-shard queries and joins get hard, so delay it as long as you can.

head: Sharding method
How
Trade-off
rows: Users 1–1M on shard A, 1M–2M on shard B.
Simple, but one shard can become a hot spot.
Even spread, but adding shards moves a lot of data unless you use consistent hashing.
A lookup table says which shard holds which key.
Flexible, but the directory is one more thing to scale and protect.

bullets: Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring, so adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys.
Pick a shard key with high cardinality and even access. A bad key, like country, creates a hot shard.
SQL gives joins and transactions. Many NoSQL stores give easy horizontal scaling and flexible shape. Choose by access pattern, not fashion.

sections.heading: Deep dive: queues, events and consistency
paragraphs: A queue lets a fast part of the system hand work to a slower part without waiting. The web request puts 'send the receipt email' on a queue and returns at once, and a worker does the email later. This smooths traffic spikes, lets you retry, and keeps failures from spreading.
bullets: At-most-once delivery can lose messages. At-least-once never loses them but can deliver twice, so consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once is really at-least-once plus idempotent handling.
Make a consumer idempotent by storing the IDs of messages already handled, or by using operations that are safe to repeat, such as 'set status to paid'.
A dead-letter queue holds messages that keep failing so they do not block the rest and can be inspected.
Backpressure: if producers outrun consumers, queues grow without limit. Limit the queue, shed load or scale consumers.
CAP theorem: during a network partition you must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets an answer). Most systems choose per feature.
Eventual consistency means replicas agree after a short delay. It is fine for likes and feeds, and not fine for payments.
Use the outbox pattern when you must update a database and publish an event reliably: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, then publish from that table.

sections.heading: Deep dive: load balancing, rate limiting and APIs

code.title: Token bucket rate limiter: allows bursts, enforces an average rate
code.text:
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_sec, capacity):
        self.rate = rate_per_sec
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.last = time.monotonic()

    def allow(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        # refill for the time that has passed
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False                    # caller returns HTTP 429

code.title: Base62 encoding for short URL codes (an ID from a counter becomes a short string)

head: Load balancing method
How it picks a server
Good for
rows: Picks the server with the fewest active connections.
Same client goes to the same server.

bullets: Rate limiting algorithms: fixed window (simple, but allows bursts at the boundary), sliding window (smoother), token bucket (allows bursts) and leaky bucket (smooths output).
Keep rate limit counters in a shared store such as Redis when you run many servers.
API design: use nouns for resources (/users/42/orders), HTTP methods for actions, plural names, consistent error shapes, pagination and versioning.
Prefer cursor pagination (?after=id) over page numbers for large or changing lists. Offsets get slow and can skip or repeat items.
Health checks let a load balancer stop sending traffic to a broken server. Add a cheap liveness check and a deeper readiness check.

sections.heading: Deep dive: reliability and observability
bullets: Timeouts everywhere: a call with no timeout can hang a whole service. Set one on every network call.
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter. Retrying instantly in lockstep makes an outage worse. Retry only operations that are safe to repeat.
A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a while so it can recover and your service stays responsive.
Graceful degradation: when a part fails, show something useful, such as cached data or a simpler page, rather than an error.
Replication and backups: a backup you have never restored is only a hope. Practise the restore.
Logs say what happened, metrics say how much and how fast, traces show the path of one request. You want all three.
Track the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Alert on symptoms users feel, not on every internal blip.
Define an SLO such as 99.9% of requests succeed in 300 ms. The remaining 0.1% is your error budget for risk and releases.

sections.heading: Worked example: design a news feed
steps: Clarify: users follow others and see a feed of recent posts. Ask about scale, freshness, ranking and media.
Estimate: say 100 million users, 10 million daily posters, and each user opens the feed 10 times a day. Reads far outweigh writes.
Choose a model. Fan-out on write: when someone posts, push the post ID into each follower's feed list. Reads are fast, writes are heavy for people with millions of followers.
Fan-out on read: build the feed when the user opens it by pulling recent posts from everyone they follow. Writes are cheap, reads are heavy.
Hybrid: fan-out on write for normal users, and fan-out on read for celebrity accounts, merging the two at read time.
Store feed lists in a cache or fast store (a list of post IDs per user), and post content in a database, fetched by ID.
Add pagination with a cursor, a ranking step if needed, and a CDN for images and video.
Discuss failure: a queue absorbs bursts of posts, workers do the fan-out, and slow followers' feeds can be built lazily.

sections.heading: Worked example: design a chat system
steps: Clarify: one-to-one and group chat, online status, history, delivery receipts, media.
Connection: use WebSockets for a long-lived two-way connection, with a fallback to long polling.
Message flow: client sends to a chat server, the server stores the message, then delivers it to the recipient's connection, or to a push notification service if offline.
Storage: messages by conversation ID and time in a store good at appends and range reads. Keep users, groups and settings in a relational database.
Ordering: give each message an ID that increases within a conversation, so clients can sort and detect gaps.
Delivery guarantees: clients acknowledge messages, the server retries until acknowledged, and duplicates are removed by message ID.
Scale: many connection servers behind a load balancer, with a registry (such as Redis) that says which server holds which user's connection.
Presence: heartbeats update a 'last seen' value. Show 'online' only if it is recent, and avoid broadcasting every change to everyone.

sections.heading: Git: the mental model
paragraphs: Git stores snapshots of your project, called commits. Each commit points to the one before it, so the history is a chain. A branch is only a movable label on a commit, which is why creating one is instant and free.

Your files live in three places: the working directory (what you edit), the staging area (what you have chosen to include in the next commit) and the repository (the saved history). Most Git commands move changes between those three places.
A remote, usually called origin, is a copy of the repository on GitHub. Pushing sends your commits there, and pulling brings other people's commits to you.

git add chooses which changes go into the next commit.
git commit saves them as a snapshot with a message.
git push sends the new commits to GitHub.

sections.heading: Git: a team workflow that works
steps: Update main: git switch main, then git pull.
Create a branch for one task: git switch -c feat/search-filter.
Make small commits, each doing one thing, with a clear message.
Push early, and open a draft pull request so others can see the direction.
Pull main into your branch regularly (or rebase on it) to avoid a big conflict at the end.
Ask for review, answer every comment, and push fixes as new commits.
Merge when the review and the checks pass, then delete the branch.
Switch back to main, pull, and start the next task on a new branch.

sections.heading: Git: good habits
bullets: One commit does one thing. If you need the word 'and' in the message, it may be two commits.
Write messages in the imperative: 'Add search filter', not 'added stuff'. Say what and why in the first line, in under about 70 characters.
Use a common style such as feat:, fix:, docs: and chore: at the start of the message, if your team does.
Never commit secrets, API keys, .env files or large generated folders. Put them in .gitignore before the first commit.
Read your own diff before every commit and every pull request.
Never rewrite history on a branch other people use. Rebase and amend only what is yours and unpushed.
Use merge when you want to keep the full history, and rebase when you want a straight line. Both are fine. Follow your team.
Never force-push to main. If you must force-push your own branch, use --force-with-lease.

sections.heading: Git: fixing a merge conflict
paragraphs: A conflict means two people changed the same lines. Git cannot guess which to keep, so it marks both and asks you. It looks scary, but it is routine.
steps: Run git status to see which files conflict.
Open each file and find the markers: <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>.
Choose what the final code should be. It may be one side, the other, or a mix. Delete the markers.
Run the code and the tests. A conflict that compiles can still be wrong.
git add the fixed files, then finish with git commit (for a merge) or git rebase --continue (for a rebase).
If you are lost, git merge --abort or git rebase --abort puts everything back as it was.

pages.intro: AI tools now write a lot of code, and companies know it. That changes what is worth learning and how you should learn it, but it does not remove the need for fundamentals. The students who do well use AI to learn faster and build more, and can still explain every line they ship.

paragraphs: A useful rule: if you could not have written it, or at least explained it, do not commit it. The AI is a fast junior who is confident and sometimes wrong. You are the senior who reviews the work.

sections.heading: Use AI to learn, not to skip learning
bullets: Try the problem first for 20–30 minutes. Then ask for a hint, not the answer. Say 'give me a hint only' or 'ask me questions until I find it'.
Ask it to explain a concept three ways: simply, with an example, and with where it breaks. Then explain it back in your own words and ask it to find the gaps.
Ask it to quiz you on a topic, and to mark your answers. It is a patient interviewer that is available at 2 a.m.
Paste an error and your code, and ask why it happens. Do not just apply the fix. Understand the cause.
Ask for a code review of your own solution: bugs, edge cases, complexity and naming. Compare it with a better solution afterwards.
Never copy a solution you cannot reproduce from a blank file a day later. That is the test of whether you learned it.
Check facts against the official docs. AI can invent functions, flags and links that do not exist.

sections.heading: Where AI help hurts you
bullets: Contests and online assessments often ban AI, and interviews often test you without it. If you only ever practised with help, you will freeze.
Pasting the problem and the answer back builds the feeling of understanding without the skill.
Accepting code you did not read creates bugs you cannot debug, and security holes you cannot see.
Your college or an employer may have rules on AI use. Read them, and say honestly when you used it.
Sharing private data, API keys, or company code in a public AI tool can leak it. Treat prompts as public unless you know otherwise.

sections.heading: A good workflow for coding with AI
steps: Write down what you want in plain words first: inputs, outputs, edge cases and what 'done' means.
Ask for a plan or a design before code, and read the plan. Fix the plan before you fix the code.
Work in small steps. One function or one change at a time, not a whole app in one go.
Read every line of the result. Run it. Ask what each part does if you do not know.
Write or ask for tests, and run them. Tests are how you check the AI, not the other way round.
Use Git: commit before a big AI change so you can undo it, and review the diff like a teammate's pull request.
When it goes in circles, stop. Start a new chat with a short summary of the problem, or debug it yourself.

bullets: Give context: the language, the framework, the version, and what the code is for.

Say the output you want: a diff, one function, a table, or a step-by-step explanation.
Ask it to say what it is unsure about, and to list assumptions it made.
Iterate. The first answer is a draft. Reply with what is wrong and what you want changed.

sections.heading: For students who want an AI/ML career
paragraphs: Building apps with models and researching or training models are different jobs. The first is a software skill and open to everyone. The second needs more mathematics and is the AI/ML role described on the Roles page.
bullets: Maths to study: linear algebra, probability and statistics, and a little calculus (gradients).
Learn classical machine learning first: regression, trees, evaluation, overfitting and cross-validation. It teaches you to think about data.
Then deep learning: neural networks, backpropagation, and transformers. Build a tiny model from scratch once.
Read a paper a week with a friend. Start with surveys and well-known papers, and reproduce one result.
Show work: a Kaggle notebook, a reproduced paper, or an honest error analysis of a model you trained.

sections.heading: AI in interviews and at work
bullets: Many interviews are still run without AI. Practise on paper or in a plain editor so you can think without help.
Some companies now allow or even test AI use. Then they judge how you prompt, check, and fix the output.
Expect questions on your projects: why this model, how you evaluated it, what it costs, and what fails. Prepare honest answers.
At work, you are still responsible for the code you merge. 'The AI wrote it' is never an answer in a review.
Be open about it. Say which parts used AI and how you verified them. Teams trust people who check.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Skipping the basics because 'AI will do it'. You then cannot tell good output from bad.
Building a chatbot wrapper with no clear problem, and no evaluation, and calling it a project.
Starting with agents or fine-tuning before you have a reliable single prompt.
Not checking cost until the bill arrives.
Trusting a confident answer. Test it, run it, and read the docs.
Switching tools every week. Pick one assistant and learn it well.
Hiding your use of AI in coursework or interviews.

steps: Choose a project you already use, or one in your language. A smaller project with active maintainers beats a huge one.

Pick a labelled issue (good first issue, documentation). Comment that you want to work on it and wait for a reply.
Fork, clone, and create a branch for the change.
Keep the change small and follow the project's style and commit rules.
Open a pull request that links the issue, explains what you changed and why, and includes screenshots or test results.
Respond to review politely and quickly. Review feedback is the best free mentoring you will get.

sections.heading: Writing a resume that gets read
bullets: One page, one column, a plain font. Recruiters and screening tools read it in seconds.
Order: contact line, education, projects, skills, experience, achievements. Freshers put projects before skills.
Write each project as: what you built, with what, and the result. Example: 'Built a leaderboard for 300 students with Next.js and PostgreSQL; refreshes scores every 5 minutes.'
Start lines with a strong verb (built, reduced, designed, led) and add a number where honest.
List only skills you can answer questions about. Group them: languages, frameworks, tools.
Link your GitHub, LeetCode or Codeforces profile and a live project. Check that every link works.
Name the file clearly, such as FirstName_LastName_Resume.pdf, and send a PDF.
Ask a senior to review it. Two reviews are better than one.

sections.heading: LinkedIn and cold outreach

Follow the companies you want and read their engineering posts.
Find an engineer or recruiter on the team. Check that they hire for your level.
Send a short message: who you are, one specific reason for this person or team, and one clear ask, such as advice or a referral for a named role.
Attach nothing on the first message, and keep it under about 100 words.
Follow up once after a week. If there is no reply, move on politely.
Thank anyone who helps, and tell them how it went.
paragraphs: A message that works is specific. 'Hi, I am a third-year student and I built a leaderboard that tracks 300 students' coding profiles. I saw your team works on data pipelines, and I am applying for the SDE intern role. Could you tell me what the team looks for in interns?' is much better than 'Please give me a referral'.

sections.heading: On the day of an interview
bullets: The night before: test your laptop, internet, charger and the meeting link. Sleep properly.
Keep a pen, paper and water close. Have your resume open.
Join five minutes early, and greet the interviewer by name.
For coding: repeat the problem, ask about inputs and limits, talk through a plan, then write.
If you are stuck, say what you have tried and ask for a small hint. Silence helps nobody.
At the end, ask two thoughtful questions about the team and the work.
Within a day, send a short thank-you note. Then write down what you were asked while it is fresh.

sections.heading: Understanding an offer
bullets: CTC is the total cost to the company. In-hand pay is lower after deductions, and some parts may be variable.
Ask what is fixed and what is variable or tied to performance, and when bonuses are paid.
Check the joining date, the location or remote policy, the bond or service agreement, and the notice period.
Read the offer letter fully before you sign. It is fine to ask questions in writing.
Do not accept two offers you cannot honour. Tell a company early if your plans change.

sections.heading: Short email templates
paragraphs: Cold email to a senior or recruiter: Hi [name], I am a [year] student at [college] and I built [one-line project]. I am interested in [role] at [company]. Could you refer me or tell me who to speak to? My resume and project link are attached. Thank you for your time.
Thank-you after an interview: Hi [name], thank you for the conversation today. I enjoyed talking about [topic]. I am keen on the role and happy to share anything else you need.
Asking for a referral: Hi [name], I saw the [role] opening at [company]. I have worked on [two relevant things]. Would you be willing to refer me? I understand if not, and thanks for reading.

sections.heading: Behavioural habits that employers notice
bullets: Reply to emails and messages within a day, even if the reply is only 'I will check and tell you by Friday'.
Arrive early to interviews and meetings, and tell people early if something changes.
Ask a clear question after trying for a reasonable time, and say what you have already tried.
Write short status updates: what you did, what is next, what is blocking you.
Accept feedback without arguing, thank the person, and show the change in your next piece of work.
Keep a short log of your wins each month. It makes your resume and performance reviews easy.

sections.heading: From an SDE's desk
paragraphs: From the hiring side, the strongest candidates were not the ones with the longest resumes. They were clear, curious and honest about what they knew.
bullets: A one-page resume with two projects you can explain deeply beats a page of tool logos.
Your first job matters less than the team: pick one where you will be reviewed and mentored.
Keep learning after the offer. The first year at work is when your growth is fastest if you ask good questions.
Stay in touch with the people you meet. Many roles are filled through someone who remembers you.
