sections.heading: A typical week

head: Activity
Rough share of time
Notes
rows: Less than most students expect. Most of the rest supports it.
You will read far more than you write, especially in your first year.
Reviewing others and responding to reviews on your work.
Bugs, alerts, questions from other teams.
New tools, the domain, the codebase.

paragraphs: These numbers vary a lot by team and level. Treat them as a feel for the job, not a rule.

sections.heading: How work flows through a team
steps: A product need becomes a ticket with a clear goal and acceptance criteria.
You or the team estimate it and break it into small pieces.
You write a short plan for anything non-trivial and discuss it with a teammate.
You make a branch, write code and tests, and open a pull request with a clear description.
Automated checks run: build, lint, tests, sometimes security scans.
Teammates review. You answer comments and push changes.
The change merges, is deployed (often behind a feature flag) and is watched in production.
You check metrics and logs, fix surprises and close the ticket.

sections.heading: Your first pull request
bullets: Pick a small, well-defined ticket. Your goal is to learn the process, not to impress anyone.
Read how others in the repo name branches, write commit messages and structure tests. Match them.
Run the full test suite and the linter locally before you push.
Describe the change: what, why, how you tested it, and anything you want the reviewer to look at.
Keep it small. A hundred lines is easy to review. A thousand will wait in a queue.
Expect comments. They are about the code, not about you.

sections.heading: Code review: giving and receiving
bullets: As an author: review your own diff first, point out the risky parts and reply to every comment.
As a reviewer: understand the goal first, then check correctness, tests, naming, error handling and security.
Ask questions instead of giving orders: 'What happens if this list is empty?'
Separate must-fix from preference. Label small style notes as 'nit'.
Approve when the change is good enough and safe, not when it matches how you would have written it.
Say what is good too. Specific praise teaches as well as criticism does.

sections.heading: A method for debugging
steps: Reproduce it. If you cannot make it fail on demand, you cannot know that you fixed it.
Read the error message and stack trace fully, from the top.
Shrink the problem: remove code, inputs or steps until the smallest failing case remains.
Form a hypothesis and test it with one change at a time. Write down what you tried.
Check recent changes. 'What changed?' solves many bugs.
Use the right tool: the debugger, logs, a profiler or a network inspector.
Fix the cause, not only the symptom, and add a test that would have caught it.
If you are stuck for more than about thirty minutes, explain it to someone else. It often unlocks the answer.

sections.heading: Estimating work
bullets: Estimates are guesses with a range. Say 'two to four days' rather than 'three days'.
Break the task into pieces under a day each. Estimating small pieces is much more accurate.
Include testing, review, deployment and surprises, not only coding.
Say early when you are late and why. Surprises hurt more than slow progress.
Compare your guesses with what actually happened, and adjust next time.

sections.heading: Writing tickets and design notes
paragraphs: A good ticket says what problem is being solved, who it affects, what 'done' looks like and what is out of scope. A good design note says the problem, the options, the choice and why, and what could go wrong. Both are short. Writing them is a senior habit that you can start now.
bullets: Lead with the why. Details are easier to follow when the goal is clear.
List alternatives you rejected, with a reason for each.
End with open questions so reviewers know where to focus.

sections.heading: Testing and quality in practice
bullets: Write tests for behaviour that would hurt if it broke: money, permissions, data loss, core flows.
Test the boundaries: empty, one, many, maximum, invalid and duplicate.
A test that fails randomly is a bug. Fix it or remove it quickly.
Use staging and feature flags to release safely and roll back fast.
Monitor after release: error rate, latency and the business number the change should move.

sections.heading: On-call and incidents
steps: Acknowledge the alert and tell the team you are looking.
Check the impact: who is affected, since when, how badly.
Stop the bleeding first: roll back, disable the flag, or scale up. Do not hunt for the perfect fix while users suffer.
Communicate in one place with short updates every so often.
Fix the root cause once the system is stable.
Write a blameless post-incident review: timeline, cause, what went well, and actions with owners.
paragraphs: Nobody expects a new engineer to run an incident alone. You will shadow first. Ask to be included early.

sections.heading: Reading an unfamiliar codebase
bullets: Start with the README, the folder layout and how to run the tests.
Pick one user-visible feature and trace it from the entry point to the database.
Use search and 'find usages' more than scrolling. Follow the data.
Read the tests. They show intended behaviour.
Read the history of a confusing file. Commit messages often explain why.
Draw a small diagram as you learn and share it. Someone will correct it, and you both learn.

sections.heading: Working with people
bullets: Ask good questions: say what you tried, what you expected and what happened.
Give updates before you are asked: done, next, blocked.
Disagree with ideas and not with people. Use evidence and offer an alternative.
Write down decisions so that nobody has to remember a meeting.
Be reliable. Doing what you said you would do is the quickest way to earn trust.
Help others. Answering a teammate's question is part of the job, and it builds your reputation.

head: Level
What changes
How to grow into it
rows: You finish well-scoped tasks with guidance and learn the codebase.
Ship reliably, ask good questions, write tests, take feedback well.
You own features end to end and work with less guidance.
Break down ambiguous work, review others, improve the system you touch.
You own larger problems across teams and make others better.
Write designs, mentor, make trade-offs clear, lead through influence.
You shape direction across many teams.
Pick the right problems, align people, keep technical quality high.

sections.heading: Habits that compound
bullets: Keep a work log of what you did and learned each week. It helps in reviews.
Read one good engineering blog post or one chapter a week.
Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it.
Take notes on mistakes, yours and others', and turn them into checklists.
Protect your time off. Tired engineers write more bugs.

glossary.meaning: A set of endpoints other programs call to use your service.
A style of API using HTTP methods and resource URLs.
A database structure that speeds up lookups at the cost of slower writes.
A group of database changes that succeed or fail together.
Fast storage for results you expect to need again.
An operation that gives the same result if repeated.
A buffer that lets work happen later, in order.
A cap on how many requests a client can make in a time window.

qa.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
qa.a: Authentication proves who you are (a login). Authorisation decides what you may do once known (permissions). Check both on every protected request.

qa.q: Why do we use database indexes, and what is the cost?
qa.a: An index lets the database find rows without scanning the table, so reads get faster. The cost is extra storage and slower writes, because the index must be updated too.

qa.q: How would you make an endpoint safe to retry?
qa.a: Make it idempotent: accept a client-supplied idempotency key, store the result of the first call, and return the same result for repeats.

qa.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
qa.a: Running one query for a list and then one more query per item. Fix it with a join or by loading the related rows in a single batched query.

qa.q: How does a cache go wrong?
qa.a: Stale data after a change, a stampede when a popular key expires, and memory growth. Use expiry, invalidate on writes, and protect hot keys.

sdeNotes: Most production problems are data problems: bad migrations, missing indexes, and inconsistent state. Treat schema changes with care.
Log with request IDs so you can follow one request across services. You will thank yourself during an incident.
Never trust input from a client. Validate on the server, always.
Make writes idempotent where you can. Retries are normal and must not double-charge anyone.
Version your API. Changing a response field breaks someone you have never met.

qa.q: What happens when you type a URL and press enter?
qa.a: The browser resolves the domain through DNS, opens a TCP and TLS connection, sends an HTTP request, receives HTML, parses it into the DOM, fetches CSS and JavaScript, builds the render tree, then lays out and paints the page.

qa.q: What is the difference between var, let and const?
qa.a: var is function-scoped and hoisted. let and const are block-scoped. const stops reassignment of the binding, but an object it holds can still change.

qa.q: What is a closure?
qa.a: A function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.

qa.q: How do you make a page faster?
qa.a: Send less JavaScript, compress and size images, cache static files, load non-critical code later, and avoid layout shifts. Measure with Lighthouse first.

qa.q: How do you make a button accessible?
qa.a: Use a real button element, give it a clear label, make it focusable with visible focus styling, and check contrast and keyboard use.

qa.q: Where would you store a login session, and why?
qa.a: Either a server-side session with an httpOnly, secure cookie, or a signed token. Cookies marked httpOnly resist theft by scripts. Avoid local storage for sensitive tokens.

qa.q: What is CORS, and why does it exist?
qa.a: Browsers block a page from reading responses from another origin unless the server allows it with CORS headers. It protects users from malicious sites reading their data.

qa.q: SSR, SSG or client rendering: how do you choose?
qa.a: SSG for content that rarely changes, SSR for pages that depend on each request, and client rendering for highly interactive parts behind a login. Mix them per page.

qa.q: How do you validate input?
qa.a: On the server always, since the client can be bypassed. Use a schema, reject bad data early, and escape output.

qa.q: How do you deploy a small full-stack app?
qa.a: Build the frontend, run the API with a managed database, keep secrets in environment variables, set up HTTPS, and add a CI check before deploy.

qa.q: Why does the app lifecycle matter?

qa.q: Why is accuracy a poor metric for imbalanced data?
qa.a: A model that always predicts the majority class can score high accuracy while finding none of the rare cases. Use precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC.

qa.q: What is the bias-variance trade-off?
qa.a: Bias is error from too-simple assumptions, and variance is error from sensitivity to the training data. Better fit lowers bias but can raise variance, so you tune for the best total.

qa.q: How does retrieval-augmented generation work?
qa.a: Split documents into chunks, embed them, store them in a vector index, retrieve the closest chunks for a question, and give them to the model as context to answer from.

qa.q: How do you know an LLM feature works?
qa.a: Build an evaluation set of realistic questions with expected answers, score outputs with checks or a rubric, track results over time, and test again after each change.

sdeNotes: Most of the work is data: cleaning, labelling, checking leaks and building a trustworthy test set.

qa.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
qa.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

qa.q: How do you handle missing data?

qa.q: Explain a join, with the main types.

qa.q: How do you check that a dashboard number is right?

qa.q: When is a result statistically meaningful?
qa.a: When the sample is large enough, the groups were fairly assigned, the effect size matters in practice, and the p-value or interval supports it. Statistical significance alone is not business value.

qa.q: How do you prevent SQL injection?
qa.a: Use parameterised queries or an ORM, never build SQL by joining strings, validate input and give the database user minimal rights.

qa.q: How should passwords be stored?
qa.a: Hash them with a slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2. Never store them in plain text or with a fast hash.

qa.q: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
qa.a: Symmetric uses one shared key and is fast. Asymmetric uses a public and private key pair, and is used for key exchange and signatures.

qa.q: What does HTTPS protect against?
qa.a: Eavesdropping and tampering on the network, and it proves the server's identity through a certificate. It does not make the app itself secure.

qa.q: Walk through what you would do after finding a vulnerability.
qa.a: Confirm it, record minimal proof, assess impact, report it responsibly to the owner with steps and a fix suggestion, and test the fix. Only test systems you have permission to test.

sdeNotes: Security is about trade-offs and risk, not perfection. Fix the biggest risks first.
Work with developers, not against them. The best fixes are easy to adopt.

qa.q: What does volatile do in C?
qa.a: It tells the compiler a variable can change outside normal flow (by hardware or an interrupt), so it must read it from memory each time and not optimise it away.

qa.q: What should an interrupt handler do?
qa.a: Be very short: set a flag, copy data, then return. Do the heavy work in the main loop. Avoid blocking calls.

qa.q: Compare I2C, SPI and UART.
qa.a: UART is asynchronous, two wires, point to point. I2C uses two shared wires with addresses for many devices at lower speed. SPI uses extra select lines but is faster.

qa.q: How do you debug a board that does not respond?
qa.a: Check power and clock first, then reset lines, then use a debugger or serial output, and a logic analyser or scope on the signals.

qa.q: Why use a watchdog timer?
qa.a: If software hangs, the watchdog resets the device so it recovers without a person, which matters for remote or safety-related devices.

sdeNotes: Read the datasheet and errata. Many bugs are in the details you skimmed.

qa.q: What is a game loop?
qa.a: A loop that repeats each frame: process input, update game state, then render. Using delta time keeps motion the same on fast and slow machines.

qa.q: How does A* pathfinding work?
qa.a: It searches a graph using the cost so far plus a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance, always expanding the most promising node. It finds the shortest path if the heuristic never overestimates.

qa.q: How do you optimise a game that drops frames?
qa.a: Profile first. Common fixes: reduce draw calls, pool objects, avoid allocations in the update loop, simplify physics and lower texture sizes.

qa.q: Why use object pooling?
qa.a: Creating and destroying many objects causes garbage collection spikes. Reusing a pool avoids allocation during gameplay.

qa.q: How do you detect a collision between two circles?
qa.a: Compare the distance between their centres with the sum of the radii. If it is smaller, they overlap. Compare squared values to avoid a square root.

qa.q: How would you improve a product you use?
qa.a: Name the user and the problem, back it with evidence, list a few ideas, pick one with a clear reason, define the metric you expect to move and how you would test it.

qa.q: How do you prioritise features?
qa.a: Score each by impact, effort, reach and confidence, check against the goal, and be open about what you are not doing.

qa.q: How do you choose success metrics?
qa.a: Tie them to the user's goal and the business goal. Pick one main metric, a few supporting ones and a guardrail so you do not harm something else.

qa.q: What do you do when engineering says it cannot be done in time?
qa.a: Ask what drives the estimate, reduce scope to the core value, look for a simpler version and agree on the trade-off with the team.

qa.q: How do you say no to a stakeholder?
qa.a: Acknowledge the need, explain the trade-off with data, offer an alternative or a later slot, and stay respectful.

qa.q: What is a reentrancy attack, and how do you prevent it?
qa.a: An external call lets an attacker call back into your function before state is updated, draining funds. Update state before external calls, use a reentrancy guard and prefer pull payments.

qa.q: Why is gas important when writing contracts?
qa.a: Each operation costs gas, and storage is costly. Efficient code lowers fees for users and avoids hitting limits.

qa.q: How is a blockchain different from a normal database?
qa.a: It is shared and replicated across many parties, append-only and secured by cryptography and consensus, so no single party can rewrite history. It is slower and costlier than a database.

qa.q: What does immutable mean for contract bugs?
qa.a: A deployed contract cannot be edited, so bugs are hard to fix. Test heavily, get audits, use upgradeable patterns with care and add emergency stops.

qa.q: How do you keep private keys safe?
qa.a: Never put them in code or a repository, use hardware wallets or secure key stores, and keep separate keys for testing and for real funds.

sdeNotes: Code is law and mistakes are permanent. Test far more than you would for a normal app.
Get an independent audit before holding real funds, and still assume bugs remain.
Gas costs are a real constraint. Design data and loops with them in mind.
Never put private keys or seed phrases in code, chats or screenshots.
Understand the economics and incentives. Many exploits are design flaws, not coding bugs.
